title: Google DeepMind Picks Four Indian Startups for Climate AI Accelerator
excerpt: Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon join the inaugural Asia-Pacific cohort, gaining access to Google's AI models and mentorship to scale climate solutions for farming and carbon markets.
body:
• Google DeepMind's AI for the Planet accelerator has named 16 organizations across Asia-Pacific to its inaugural cohort, including four from India.
  • The Indian participants — Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon — apply AI to smallholder farming, carbon credits, agroforestry and biochar.
  • The three-month programme began with a bootcamp in Singapore and gives teams access to Google AI models such as AnthroKrishi and AlphaEarth Foundations, plus technical mentorship.
  • Google says the accelerator is meant to move climate projects from pilots toward wider deployment.

Four Indian startups join Google's climate AI accelerator

Google DeepMind has selected four Indian startups for the inaugural Asia-Pacific cohort of its AI for the Planet accelerator, a three-month programme giving climate-focused teams access to Google's AI models, technical support and mentorship. The 16-organization cohort spans Australia, Indonesia, Japan, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea, Thailand and India, and opened with a bootcamp in Singapore this week, according to MIT Sloan Management Review India.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=YOy8FjkXajY

The four Indian participants all work at the intersection of agriculture and climate data. Terrastack combines satellite imagery with agricultural data to deliver plot-level intelligence for smallholder farmers. Varaha Climate applies remote sensing and AI to verify regenerative farming and carbon-removal projects that can generate carbon credits for farmers. Farmers for Forests uses AI-enabled drones to measure the carbon and biodiversity impact of smallholder agroforestry, while Climitra Carbon uses geo-spatial AI to verify the removal of invasive plant species and their conversion into biochar.

Context & Background

The accelerator is Google's bet that advanced AI models can do their most useful climate work far from chatbots — in domains where data is difficult to collect or interpret, such as land use, ecosystems and agricultural productivity. Participants get access to specialized Google models including AnthroKrishi, ForestCast, AlphaEarth Foundations, SpeciesNet and Perch.

The announcement sits inside a wider sustainability push Google detailed on September 10: scaling its Solar API to cover more than 300 million rooftops in India, a new 150-megawatt solar agreement with ReNew Power in Rajasthan, a methane-reduction project with Mitti Labs for rice farmers in Telangana, and expanded research areas for the Google Center for Climate Technology. The accelerator cohort, welcomed earlier that week, is the startup-ecosystem piece of that strategy.

"These five initiatives demonstrate how combining foundational research, public partnerships, and direct support for local innovators can accelerate technological solutions that foster a sustainable, climate-resilient future for India."

— Vrushali Gaud, Director of Climate Operations, Google

Impact & Analysis

The cohort's composition says something about where climate AI is actually useful: measurement. Carbon markets live or die on verification — proving that a tonne of carbon was really removed — and that measurement has historically been expensive, manual and slow. Satellite models, drones and geo-spatial AI attack exactly that bottleneck. If Varaha Climate or Farmers for Forests can verify carbon outcomes cheaply and credibly, smallholder farmers gain access to carbon income that was previously out of reach.

Google frames the programme as deployment-focused rather than research-focused. The company said the accelerator is intended to "help participants move their existing projects toward wider deployment." That distinction matters: the teams arrive with working projects, and the three months are about scaling them. Whether AI-verified carbon credits and plot-level farm intelligence survive contact with real-world Indian agriculture — fragmented landholdings, patchy connectivity, thin margins — is the test the programme sets up.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the cohort is a window into how India's climate-tech story is maturing. The problems these startups tackle — smallholder productivity, verifiable carbon markets, land restoration — are India-first, but the tooling is global: satellite constellations, foundation models, drone hardware. Indian-origin engineers and researchers working in climate AI abroad will recognize the playbook, and the accelerator creates a natural bridge for diaspora talent, mentors and capital to plug into teams building for Indian conditions.

What's Next

The three-month programme runs through the end of the year, with product refinement, architecture reviews and mentoring aimed at preparing the teams for scaled deployment. The signal to watch is whether any of the four convert the accelerator's model access and mentorship into deployments beyond their current pilots. Google, meanwhile, keeps expanding its India climate portfolio — from rooftop solar data to rice-methane credits — suggesting the accelerator is one piece of a longer infrastructure bet.
